source.title: Single Character Perturbations Break LLM Alignment
source.authors: Leon Lin; Hannah Brown; Kenji Kawaguchi; M. Shieh

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether single-character changes to chat templates can bypass refusal behavior, using attack-success rates rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures refusal failure/harmful-output rates after adding characters to chat templates. It also reports next-token overlap and token-type observations, but these do not measure per-token KL across response positions. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures refusal failure on AdvBench after appending one character, a minimal suffix, to the end of chat templates. That is a different method aimed at V4's question: whether changing what precedes the response opening defeats refusal. It reports with/without-space ASRs for 11 chat models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a single appended space at the template end reliably breaks alignment in most open models (not Llama-2/3). They attribute this to single-space tokens preceding numbers in tokenized pretraining data, which pushes the model toward lists. They add that the final token position matters most, and that space-prepended fine-tuning helps but is no full defense.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses single-character perturbations to chat templates, rather than harmful-example fine-tuning or measuring aligned-versus-base per-token KL. It includes a LIMA fine-tuning experiment only as a defense against the character attack.
record.method_sensitivity: The attack depends on insertion location: appending the space to the end is much more effective than inserting it at the start, before the user input, or after the user input. The study also reports substantial differences across models and characters; fine-tuning examples with spaces reduces the trailing-space attack rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Appending a space changes the first predicted token and gives low top-k next-token overlap in affected models. In affected models the first token shifts to numerals, starting lists; Llama-2/3 overlap stays near 100% at k=100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Template-end perturbations defeat refusal by shifting the first response token distribution, consistent with refusal hinging on the opening token.

record.problems: The primary evaluation marks outputs as harmful based on refusal-word matching; the authors manually checked 10 outputs per model and report that this evaluation was accurate for 74/80. Their additional manual assessment found 6/80 marked successes were not harmful or had other issues. The results are limited to English prompts and open-source models. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper gives inconsistent Falcon space-attack values (84.0 in Table 1 and 87.0 in Appendix Table 5) and describes Llama-3 as unaffected although Table 1 lists 3.0.
record.rows_left_out: The appendix reports many additional single-character ASRs in Tables 5–7; these are omitted to prioritize the main space results, model differences, fine-tuning result, and insertion-position controls within the row limit. Figure 3 and Appendix Figure 7 contain further character and template-pair results, but their values are figure-only and are not separately extracted. The GSM8K performance comparison concerns task performance rather than harmful-response behavior. Tokenization/pretraining frequency results do not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant response start; decoding changes; multi-token optimized suffixes. The paper runs GCG only with suffix length 1.
Benign LIMA fine-tuning is run, but harmful compliance without the attack is not reported.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Localization of safety in weights or ranks.
Whether the alignment data or objective causes shallowness. The paper attributes its attack to pretraining tokenization contexts instead.
Training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens. Space-prepended LIMA fine-tuning is a format-robustness defense, not deepening.

missing.what: Single-token GCG search on Vicuna-7B: the most frequently selected tokens give ASR 12–81 versus a 3.0 baseline.
First-token type shift to numerals with space appended; without space no model starts with a number.
Llama-2 shows nonzero ASR (up to 31–37) for some non-Latin single-character tokens. This qualifies the Llama-2 challenge, though Tables 5–7 are declared left out.

record.verdict_notes: Success is scored by refusal-keyword matching. A manual check found 6/80 'successes' were not truly harmful, so ASRs may overstate harmful compliance. Falcon's space ASR is inconsistent: 84 in Table 1 versus 87 in Table 5. Neither paper is an original source. Greedy decoding was used throughout, and there are no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and its effect on harmful compliance.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance without a template attack.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions. The study examines next-token changes and overlap, not this measure.

Prefilling a compliant opening and decoding changes. The study tests single-character template perturbations, including trailing spaces and punctuation; it does not test the full range of suffix attacks.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether the training data or objective causes safety to be shallow. The study investigates why its character attack works, not the origin of shallow safety training.
Training safety beyond the first tokens and testing whether that deepening holds up.

rows.subject: Vicuna-7B fine-tuned on LIMA samples without prepended spaces
rows.operation_detail: Append a space to the end of the model template after fine-tuning on 1,000 LIMA instructions for 10 epochs.
rows.measure: Attack success rate (ASR)
rows.note: The reported result is attack success after the specified fine-tuning.
rows.check: No baseline is given for the fine-tuned model. ASR of 99 after LIMA LoRA fine-tuning shows the attack survives benign fine-tuning. The paper reports no no-attack ASR for this model.

rows.measure: Attack success rate (ASR)
rows.note: Authors say this fine-tuning makes the model significantly more robust, but it remains vulnerable to other punctuation tokens.
rows.check: This is a defense condition. ASR is 23 versus 99, and the no-attack baseline for the fine-tuned model is not stated.

rows.subject: 7B models (reported across affected models)

rows.measure: Overlap in top-k predicted next tokens
rows.note: The text reports very low overlap for affected models, especially Vicuna and MPT, and almost 100% overlap at k=100 for Llama-2 and Llama-3. This is not per-token KL across response positions.
rows.check: This is a next-token overlap between perturbed and unperturbed inputs, not aligned-vs-base per-token KL. The values are figure-only.

tranche.reason: Single-character template perturbations and refusal-matching ASR test V4 through a different method.

source_check.notes: ASR uses refusal-substring matching; manual inspection found 74/80 outputs correctly classified, so ASR is not independently verified harmful compliance.
